⭐️ SEC eyes enforcement action over prediction market insider trading 

🔖 The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has warned that prediction markets offering contracts linked to corporate earnings and business performance could face enforcement action over insider trading, fraud and market manipulation. SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency was monitoring activity on prediction platforms and expected to pursue potential securities violations. He added that enforcement activity was likely “in the future, for sure,” although he did not identify a particular company or announce new charges.

➡️ Woodcock’s comments centered on contracts that allow traders to bet on financial results or key performance indicators, commonly known as KPIs. Such products can involve outcomes tied to quarterly earnings, sales figures or other measures of a listed company’s business performance. The SEC oversees securities markets, while the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates many derivatives contracts. Prediction markets can raise questions about which agency has authority when a contract’s outcome depends on a publicly traded company.

🔔 The regulator has already approved a Cboe Global Markets proposal involving binary options tied to corporate performance measures. The contracts allow traders to take positions on outcomes such as Citigroup’s earnings per share or Apple’s iPhone sales revenue. The decision addressed Cboe’s particular products and did not establish that every prediction contract involving a company’s performance automatically falls under SEC jurisdiction.

The Associated Press alleges that Russian reconnaissance satellites supplied intelligence for strikes on Saudi oil and military infrastructure by Yemen's Ansar Allah and Iraqi resistance groups.

The claim rests on an analysis by AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence, a Geneva-based private firm founded by Nawaf Obaid, a former security adviser to the Saudi government. The firm says it tracked 72 Russian government and military satellites and examined 40 missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia between July 1 and October 19. Obaid calls it a "100% match": in every case, Russian satellites were orbiting over the targets in the days before and after the strike.

Examples cited include the September 10 drone strikes from Iraq on three pumping stations of the East-West Pipeline, which forced a temporary shutdown, and the attack on King Fahd Air Base that damaged an Italian fighter jet in a hangar.

According to AP, Iranian advisers on the ground processed the data and passed targeting information to allies. Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly said Iran and Ansar Allah get intelligence from "elements in Russia and China, even commercial elements sometimes." An unnamed official briefed on Saudi investigations went further, also linking Russian satellites to Iran's March strikes on Prince Sultan Air Base and a CIA unit at the US Embassy in Riyadh.

A vulnerability in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) condition.
This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition. 

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

Crypto Idea

Gold is widely considered the ultimate safe-haven asset. But something interesting is happening right now. Despite high oil prices, geopolitical tensions, and a falling stock market, gold itself has dropped to a three-month low, losing around 4% in a single week.

The reason is pretty simple. High oil prices are fueling inflation again. The higher inflation goes, the more likely the Fed is to keep interest rates elevated or raise them further. And gold doesn't generate any interest income on its own. When bonds and the dollar start offering more attractive returns, some money flows in that direction instead.

There's a second factor, too. When markets sell off sharply, investors sometimes have to sell just about everything to cover losses and meet margin calls. That's why even gold can temporarily fall alongside stocks during periods of severe market stress. And that's exactly the kind of price action we're seeing right now.

And here's the key takeaway. A safe-haven asset isn't necessarily an asset that rises during every crisis. Gold performs well against some risks and less well against others. It can provide protection against currency problems, debt crises, and financial instability, while simultaneously coming under pressure from high interest rates and a strong dollar.

That's why it's worth rethinking gold as an all-purpose hedge. Before buying any safe-haven asset, it is important to first understand exactly which risk needs to be hedged. Because the very same crisis can make gold either the best-performing asset in portfolio or, at least temporarily, one of the worst.
